results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No, creatures phasing back in do not trigger enter-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing does not cause a permanent to change zones; it only changes its status from 'phased out' to 'phased in' while it remains on the battlefield. Rule [702.26d] explicitly states that the phasing event does not cause a permanent to leave or enter the battlefield, so zone-change triggers like enters-the-battlefield abilities do not trigger when a permanent phases in. Additionally, [702.26j] confirms that abilities triggering when a permanent becomes attached or unattached also do not trigger on phasing, reinforcing that phasing is not treated as a zone change.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text: When a creature with both trample and deathtouch assigns combat damage, deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of damage lethal to a blocking creature. This means the attacking creature’s controller needs to assign only 1 damage to each blocking creature to satisfy lethal damage, and the rest of the creature’s power can be assigned as trample damage to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle. For example, a 5/5 with trample and deathtouch blocked by a 3/3 can assign 1 damage to the blocker (lethal due to deathtouch) and 4 damage to the defending player. This is because [702.2c] states that any nonzero amount of combat damage from a source with deathtouch is considered lethal for determining excess damage, and [702.19b] allows excess damage after lethal to be assigned to the attacked player or permanent. The same principle applies to trample over planeswalkers under [702.19c], where after assigning lethal to blockers (1 damage each with deathtouch) and at least the planeswalker’s loyalty, further excess can go to the planeswalker’s controller. Note that if the blocking creature has protection or damage prevention, the attacker must still assign at least 1 damage to it (as lethal) even if that damage will be prevented, per the example in [702.19b].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: No, storm is a triggered ability, and triggered abilities on the stack are not spells. They cannot be countered by effects that counter only spells, but they can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. See rule [113.9].

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text: No, you cannot use a card with a hybrid mana symbol in a Commander deck if your commander’s color identity does not include all the colors of that hybrid symbol. Under [903.5c], each card in a Commander deck must have a color identity that is a subset of the commander’s color identity. A hybrid mana symbol such as {R/G} is all of its component colors (red and green) per [107.4e]. Therefore, a card with {R/G} in its mana cost or rules text has a color identity that includes both red and green. If your commander’s color identity is only red (or only green), that card’s color identity is not a subset, so it cannot be included. This applies to any hybrid symbol: for example, a card with {W/U} has a color identity of white and blue, and cannot go in a deck whose commander is only white or only blue. The same rule applies to cards brought from outside the game via effects like wishes, as stated in [903.11a].

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to the untap step. According to rule [502.4], no player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated or resolve. Any triggered abilities that trigger during this step are held until the next time a player would receive priority, which is usually during the upkeep step (rule [503.1a]). The untap step is one of the steps in which no players receive priority, as specified in rule [500.3]. Therefore, you cannot take any actions during the untap step itself.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text: Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. According to rule [508.1k], a creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. The end of combat step is part of the combat phase (see [End of Combat Step]), so the combat phase has not yet ended during this step. Rule [511.3] confirms that creatures are removed from combat only after the end of combat step ends, when the combat phase is over. Therefore, throughout the end of combat step, creatures that were declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking (per [508.4]) are still attacking creatures. This matters for effects that refer to attacking creatures or that trigger 'at end of combat' (see [511.2]), which trigger as the step begins while the creatures are still attacking.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text: No, you do not cast lands. Lands are never cast as spells. Playing a land is a special action that does not use the stack, as defined by [305.1], [505.6b], and [701.18a]. A land card has no mana cost [202.1b], and if an object is both a land and another card type, it can only be played as a land, not cast as a spell [305.9], [300.2a]. The term "play a card" can mean either playing a land or casting a spell, but lands specifically are played, not cast [701.18b], [601.1a].

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text: No, you cannot sacrifice an evoked creature before its evoke triggered ability resolves. The evoke ability (rule 702.74a) consists of two parts: a static ability that lets you cast the spell for its evoke cost, and a triggered ability that says "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it." This triggered ability goes on the stack the next time a player would receive priority after the creature enters the battlefield (rule 603.3d). Until that triggered ability resolves, you have no priority to sacrifice the creature (unless another effect specifically allows a special action, such as discarding Circling Vultures per rule 116.2e, but no such special action exists for sacrificing). The sacrifice required by the evoke trigger is mandatory and happens only when that trigger resolves. You cannot preemptively sacrifice the creature yourself before that trigger resolves, because you do not receive priority between the creature entering and the trigger being put on the stack, and even after the trigger is on the stack, sacrificing the creature would not remove the trigger (rule 113.7a: the ability exists independently of its source). The only way to sacrifice the creature before the evoke trigger resolves is if another spell or ability you control gives you priority and an opportunity to sacrifice, but that would be a separate action, not a way to avoid the evoke sacrifice itself.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text: Yes. Rule [113.10b] states that an effect which removes an ability will state that the object “loses” that ability, and that such effects remove all instances of it. Keyword abilities (defined in [702.1] as abilities whose name is listed as a keyword) are a subset of abilities. Therefore, if an effect causes a permanent to lose all abilities, it removes all keyword abilities as well. For example, [702.22b] explicitly confirms that losing banding also removes all “bands with other” abilities, and [702.11e] confirms that losing hexproof removes all “hexproof from [quality]” abilities. The layer system ([613.1f]) applies ability-removing effects in layer 6, which includes both keyword and non-keyword abilities.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes, you can draw cards even if you already have a number of cards in your hand equal to or greater than your maximum hand size. Drawing cards is not prohibited by being at or above the maximum hand size. The maximum hand size only matters during the cleanup step of your turn, when you must discard down to that number (see rule [402.2] and [514.1]). The act of drawing itself is unaffected by your current hand size. For example, if your maximum hand size is seven and you have seven cards in hand, you may still draw a card; you will then have eight cards in hand, and you will need to discard down to seven during the cleanup step. This is true for any number of cards drawn, as long as you can actually draw them (e.g., your library has cards). If your library is empty and you are forced to draw, you draw the remaining cards (none) and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (see [104.3c]). Note that some effects may replace or prevent draws, but the maximum hand size itself does not prevent drawing.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text: When a planeswalker on the battlefield has 0 loyalty counters, it is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This is because a planeswalker's loyalty on the battlefield equals the number of loyalty counters on it [306.5c], and if that number is 0, state-based action [704.5i] applies: the planeswalker is put into its owner's graveyard [306.9]. This check happens the next time a player would receive priority [104.3b], unless an effect ends the turn or combat phase, in which case state-based actions are checked immediately without priority being given [724.1c][724.2c]. Note that damage dealt to a planeswalker removes that many loyalty counters [120.3c][306.8], which can cause its loyalty to become 0. If a planeswalker's loyalty is ever 0 or less (e.g., due to removing more counters than it has), the same state-based action applies—it is put into the graveyard. This rule applies in all game formats, including multiplayer and Commander; the planeswalker's owner is the player who put it into play, and the graveyard is that player's graveyard. The provided rules do not cover the case of a planeswalker having negative loyalty counters (e.g., -1), but since loyalty is defined as the number of loyalty counters on it [306.5c], and counters cannot be negative, the only relevant threshold is 0—if the number of counters is 0, the planeswalker is put into the graveyard.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text: No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" is defined as being put into a graveyard from the battlefield, but it applies only to creatures and planeswalkers, as stated in the rule for "Dies." The rule explicitly says: "A creature or planeswalker ‘dies’ if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield." Non-creature artifacts are neither creatures nor planeswalkers, so they cannot die. If a non-creature artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, it is not considered to have died; it is simply put there (e.g., by being destroyed, sacrificed, or via a state-based action). This distinction matters for abilities that trigger on "dies," such as "Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life"—such abilities would not trigger from a non-creature artifact leaving the battlefield. The rule [701.8b] further clarifies that being destroyed is a specific way a permanent can be put into a graveyard, but "dies" is a separate term limited to creatures and planeswalkers.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text: If you are instructed to draw a card (or it is a turn-based action during your draw step) and your library is empty, you attempt to draw. Since there are no cards in your library, you cannot actually put any card into your hand. However, the attempt to draw from an empty library causes you to lose the game the next time a player would receive priority, as a state-based action. This is true whether the draw is mandatory (e.g., the draw step) or optional (e.g., an effect that offers a choice to draw). If an effect replaces the draw (e.g., with dredge), the replacement is applied even if the library is empty, but if the replacement itself is impossible (e.g., dredge requires milling cards and there are fewer than the required number), the draw attempt still happens and you lose. The key zones involved are your library (empty) and your hand (no card added). The relevant steps are the draw step (for turn-based draws) or the resolution of a spell/ability (for effect-based draws).

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat ([506.1]). As the defending player, you receive priority at the beginning of most steps after turn-based actions and triggered abilities are handled ([117.3a]). Specifically:

- **Beginning of combat step**: After the turn-based action of choosing a defending player (if applicable, [507.1]) and any beginning-of-combat triggers are put on the stack, the active player gets priority first ([117.3a]). You (the defending player) will get priority later in that step after the active player passes.
- **Declare attackers step**: After attackers are declared and any triggers are put on the stack, the active player gets priority first; you get priority later.
- **Declare blockers step**: After blockers are declared and triggers are put on the stack, the active player gets priority first; you get priority later.
- **Combat damage step**: After combat damage is assigned and dealt (a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, [510.1], [510.2]), the active player gets priority first ([117.3a]); you get priority later.
- **End of combat step**: This step has no turn-based actions ([511.1]). The active player gets priority first ([117.3a]); you get priority later.

In a multiplayer game where all opponents are defending players (e.g., the Attack Multiple Players option), the same priority order applies: active player first, then you in turn order ([802.2], [802.5]). In a team game using shared team turns, the active team assigns damage first, then the defending team, but priority still follows the same pattern ([805.10f]).

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities do not use the stack [605.3b][605.4a][113.4]. Because they don't go on the stack, they cannot be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to [605.3b][605.4a]. Instead, a mana ability resolves immediately after it is activated [605.3b][405.6c]. This applies to both activated mana abilities (e.g., tapping a land for mana) and triggered mana abilities (e.g., an enchantment that adds mana when a land is tapped) [605.3b][605.4a]. The only actions that can be taken while a mana ability is resolving are activating other mana abilities or taking special actions (such as turning a face-down creature face up) if allowed by the game state [117.1d][702.61b].

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text: No, you cannot respond to a cost being paid. Paying a cost is part of the process of casting a spell, activating an ability, or taking a special action (such as declaring attackers or blockers). These processes do not use the stack, and players do not receive priority during the payment of costs. Specifically, when a player pays costs, they follow the steps in rules 601.2f–h (for casting spells) or the declaration steps in rules 508.1f–j and 509.1e–f (for combat). During these steps, no player gets priority to respond; the game only allows the active player to activate mana abilities if the cost includes mana (see [508.1i], [509.1e]), but that is part of the cost payment itself, not a response. Once costs are fully paid, the spell or ability goes on the stack, and then players receive priority to respond to the spell or ability itself (not to the cost). For example, if a player sacrifices a creature to pay an additional cost, you cannot respond to that sacrifice because it is part of the cost payment, which occurs without the stack. Rule [118.10] also confirms that each payment applies to only one spell or ability, and the resolution of a spell or ability does not pay another cost, reinforcing that cost payment is a discrete, non-interruptible action.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text: Layers are a system the game uses to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object's characteristics. The process starts with the object's base characteristics (printed on a card, or defined by the effect that created a token or copy) [613.1]. Then, all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers, in a fixed order [613.1]. The layers are: Layer 1: rules and effects that modify copiable values (including copy effects) [613.1a]; Layer 2: control-changing effects; Layer 3: text-changing effects [613.1c]; Layer 4: type-changing effects (card type, subtype, supertype) [613.1d]; Layer 5: color-changing effects [613.1e]; Layer 6: ability-adding, keyword counters, ability-removing, and effects that say an object can't have an ability [613.1f]; Layer 7: power- and toughness-changing effects, which itself has sublayers: 7a (characteristic-defining abilities that set power/toughness), 7b (power/toughness-setting effects), and 7c (effects that modify power/toughness without setting them, such as +1/+1 counters or +X/+X until end of turn) [613.4a]. Within each layer or sublayer, effects are applied in timestamp order, unless a dependency exists (where one effect must be applied before another for the second to work correctly) [613.8][613.8a]. If an effect applies in multiple layers (e.g., an effect that both changes color and gives +1/+1), each part applies in its appropriate layer [613.6]. The game applies these layers automatically and continuously [613.5].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text: The legend rule is a state-based action that applies when a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name. When this condition is checked (before a player would receive priority, per [117.2d]), that player chooses one of those permanents to keep, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. This is defined in [704.5j] and applies to any permanent with the supertype “legendary” ([205.4d]). The rule does not target, does not use the stack, and is not optional—it happens automatically. For example, if you control two copies of the legendary creature “Ghalta, Primal Hunger,” you must choose one to keep and put the other into its owner’s graveyard. Note that the legend rule is distinct from the world rule (for permanents with supertype “world,” [704.5k]) and the Role rule (for Aura enchantments with subtype “Role,” [704.5y]). The obsolete planeswalker uniqueness rule no longer exists; planeswalkers are now legendary and subject to the legend rule ([306.4]).

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text: Your creature dies as a state-based action the next time state-based actions are checked, which occurs just before a player would receive priority. Specifically, after lethal damage is marked on the creature (e.g., from a spell like Lightning Bolt), the game does not immediately destroy it. Instead, the next time a player would get priority—such as after the spell or ability that dealt the damage finishes resolving—the game checks state-based actions. If the creature has damage marked on it greater than or equal to its toughness, it is destroyed as a state-based action at that point. This happens before any player receives priority, and state-based actions do not use the stack. See rules [704.3], [704.5g], [117.2d], [117.5], and [405.6f]. Note that if an effect ends the turn or the combat phase (e.g., Mandate of Peace), state-based actions are checked as part of that process as well (see [724.1c] and [724.2c]). Damage is not removed until the cleanup step ([514.2], [703.4p]), so the creature remains marked and subject to destruction until then, unless it regenerates or the damage is otherwise removed earlier.

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text: No, you cannot cast your commander from exile unless an effect explicitly allows it. The default rules for casting a commander only permit casting it from the command zone (rule 903.8). While a commander retains its designation in exile (rule 903.3d), there is no general rule allowing a player to cast a commander from exile. However, if an effect (such as a spell or ability) specifically says you may cast a card from exile, and that card is your commander, you may do so, provided you follow all normal timing and permission rules (rule 601.3f). The commander tax from rule 903.8 only applies when casting from the command zone, not from exile. Additionally, if your commander would be put into exile, you may choose to move it to the command zone instead via the state-based action in rule 903.9a, which would then allow you to cast it from the command zone under rule 903.8.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
During the cleanup step, the following occurs in order:

1. **Turn-based actions** (rule [703.4p]): The active player discards down to their maximum hand size (if necessary), then all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. These happen simultaneously and do not use the stack (rule [514.2]).

2. **State-based actions and triggered abilities** (rules [514.3a], [704.3]): Normally, no player gets priority during the cleanup step. However, after the turn-based actions, the game checks for state-based actions. If any are performed, they are done simultaneously, and the check repeats. If no state-based actions are performed, the game checks for triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”). If any triggered abilities are waiting, they are put on the stack, and then the active player gets priority. Players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins.

3. **If no state-based actions and no triggered abilities** (rule [514.3a]): No player gets priority, and the cleanup step ends immediately.

4. **If an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step** (rule [724.1d]): A new cleanup step begins.

5. **If an effect ends the turn earlier** (rule [724.1f]): The game skips to the cleanup step. During that cleanup step, if any triggered abilities triggered since the turn-ending process began, they are put on the stack, the active player gets priority, and players can cast spells and activate abilities. Then another cleanup step occurs before the turn finally ends. If no triggered abilities triggered, no player gets priority during that cleanup step.

Key zones involved: The battlefield (permanents), the stack (for triggered abilities and spells), and the graveyard (for discarded cards). The cleanup step is part of the ending phase (rule [Cleanup Step]).

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text:
State-based actions are checked immediately before a player would receive priority, as a single event, and are repeated until no more state-based actions are performed. This occurs at the start of each step or phase (after any turn-based actions for that step/phase), during the cleanup step (with a special exception that may give priority), and also when an effect ends the turn or ends the combat phase (in which case no player gets priority afterward). Specifically:

- **Before priority**: Whenever a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously, then repeats until none are performed. Then triggered abilities are put on the stack, and the process repeats until no state-based actions and no triggered abilities remain, at which point the player gets priority. [704.3][117.5]
- **At the beginning of a step or phase**: Turn-based actions for that step/phase are dealt with first, then state-based actions are checked before triggered abilities and priority. [703.3]
- **During the cleanup step**: Normally no player gets priority, but if state-based actions would be performed or triggered abilities are waiting, those are performed, then the active player gets priority. [514.3a]
- **When an effect ends the turn or combat phase**: State-based actions are checked, but no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack. [724.1c][724.2c]

State-based actions are automatic, do not use the stack, and are not controlled by any player. [704.1][704.1a][704.2][405.6f] They are distinct from turn-based actions (which happen automatically when steps/phases begin or end) and triggered abilities (which watch for game states and use the stack). [117.2c][117.2d][405.6e]

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You can concede a game at any time. This is a fundamental rule that overrides all other rules and card effects. Specifically, rule [104.3a] states that a player can concede at any time, and rule [101.1] explicitly notes that the only exception to the rule that a card can override the rules is that a player can concede at any time. Conceding does not use the stack [405.6g] and cannot be prevented by another player, even if that player controls you [723.6]. In Two-Headed Giant, if a player concedes, their entire team leaves the game immediately and loses [810.8b]. The concession takes effect immediately, regardless of the game state, phase, or any other ongoing effects or spells on the stack.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text: The active player is the player whose turn it is. This is defined in rule [102.1]. During a turn, the active player is the one currently taking that turn; for example, during the combat phase, the active player is the attacking player ([506.2b]). In multiplayer games using the shared team turns option, the active team (the team whose turn it is) replaces the concept of a single active player, and any ability referring to 'the active player' is chosen by the ability's controller from among the active team's players ([805.9], [805.4a]). To determine the active player at any moment, simply identify whose turn it is.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: After a spell (other than a mana ability) resolves, the active player receives priority, regardless of who cast the spell. This is stated in rule [117.3b]: "The active player receives priority after a spell or ability (other than a mana ability) resolves." The identity of the caster does not change this rule. Therefore, even if a nonactive player casts a spell, once that spell resolves, the active player gets priority first. If the spell is countered or otherwise leaves the stack without resolving, the same rule applies: after the spell or ability finishes (e.g., a counter spell resolves), the active player gets priority. The only exception is if a special action is taken (rule [116.3]) or if a spell or ability is cast/activated (rule [117.3c]), in which case the player who took that action receives priority afterward, but that is a separate event from the resolution of a spell cast by another player.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: After the active player casts a spell, the active player receives priority first. This is because rule [117.3c] states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Additionally, rule [117.3b] specifies that the active player receives priority after a spell or ability resolves, but casting a spell does not involve resolution—it is the act of putting the spell on the stack. Since the active player had priority to cast the spell, they retain priority immediately after casting it, unless a rule or effect states otherwise (e.g., a spell that instructs an opponent to take an action during casting, as per [601.7b], does not change who gets priority afterward). The active player then has the option to pass priority to the next player in turn order (usually the non-active player in a two-player game).

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes, you can hold priority to cast more spells after casting one, but only if you had priority before casting the first spell. According to rule [601.2i], once the steps of casting a spell are completed, if the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority again. This means you, as the controller, receive priority immediately after your spell becomes cast, and you may then cast additional spells or activate abilities before any other player gets a chance to respond. However, this only applies if you were the player with priority when you began casting the first spell. If you did not have priority (e.g., because another player was casting a spell or an ability was resolving), you cannot cast spells at all until you receive priority through normal game actions (such as a spell resolving or a phase change). The key rule is [601.2i]: 'If the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority.' This is the mechanism for 'holding priority'—you retain priority after your own spell is cast, allowing you to cast more spells in succession before passing priority to opponents.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text: Lore counters are put on Sagas in two ways: (1) as a turn-based action immediately after the active player’s precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities (see [703.4f], [505.4]); (2) as a replacement effect upon entering the battlefield—a Saga without read ahead enters with one lore counter ([714.3a]), while a Saga with read ahead enters with a chosen number of lore counters between one and its final chapter number ([714.3b], [702.155b]). The turn-based action does not use the stack ([714.3c], [505.4]).

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is a triggered ability created by the effects of resolving spells or abilities, replacement effects, or static abilities that allow a player to take an action. It contains 'when,' 'whenever,' or 'at' and triggers later based on a specified event. Its source and controller are determined by the rules in 603.7d–f, and it typically triggers only once unless it has a stated duration (603.7b). The value of X in such an ability, if undefined in its text, is the same as the value of X from the spell or ability that created it (107.3n).

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instant and sorcery spells) can have abilities. While on the stack, an instant or sorcery spell is an object that retains all the characteristics of the card associated with it, including any abilities printed on that card. These abilities are called spell abilities and function only while the spell is on the stack, as per rule [113.6]. For example, an instant spell with the text "Counter target spell" has a spell ability that instructs its controller to counter a target spell when it resolves. Additionally, some static abilities on instant or sorcery spells apply while the spell is on the stack, such as those that modify how the spell can be cast (e.g., "You may cast this spell without paying its mana cost"), as noted in rules [604.5] and [113.6e]. However, non-permanent spells do not have abilities that function on the battlefield because they are not permanents; their abilities only matter during the casting and resolution process on the stack.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Rule [702.61b] explicitly states that players may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. This is an exception to the general restriction imposed by split second (rule [702.61a]), which normally prevents players from casting other spells or activating non-mana abilities. Mana abilities are defined in rule [605.1] and follow special rules: they don’t use the stack (rule [605.3b]) and can be activated even without priority in certain circumstances (rule [605.3a]). During the resolution of a spell or ability, rule [608.2g] also confirms that players may activate mana abilities when instructed to pay mana. Therefore, the presence of a split-second spell does not prevent you from activating mana abilities.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: Counterspell resolves first, and Divination does not resolve. When all players pass priority, the top object on the stack resolves ([608.1]). Since Counterspell is on top of the stack, it resolves first. Counterspell's effect is to counter target spell ([701.6a]), which removes Divination from the stack and puts it into its owner's graveyard ([701.6a], [608.2n]). A countered spell does not resolve and none of its effects occur ([701.6a]). Divination is no longer on the stack when it would be the next object to resolve, so it never resolves. The stack is a zone; spells on it are objects ([112.1]). Once Counterspell resolves and counters Divination, Divination leaves the stack and is not available to resolve later.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 1 damage to Vampire Nighthawk (the blocker) before any excess damage can trample over to the defending player. This is because deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of combat damage lethal [702.2c], and trample requires lethal damage to be assigned to all blocking creatures before excess damage can be assigned to the defending player [702.19b]. Since Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, 1 damage is lethal, so you assign 1 damage to it and the remaining 3 damage (from Charging Rhino’s 4 power) to the defending player. Note that the deathtouch on Vampire Nighthawk does not affect how much damage you must assign to it; it only matters that the source of damage (Charging Rhino) does not have deathtouch itself. The deathtouch on the blocker is irrelevant for trample assignment—only the attacker’s deathtouch would reduce the lethal threshold to 1 [702.2c].

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers **after** the cascaded spell is put onto the stack, but **before** that spell resolves. Here's the detailed sequence:

1. You cast Shardless Agent. Its cascade ability triggers (rule 702.85a: "When you cast this spell...").
2. Cascade resolves first (Shardless Agent ruling #1: cascade resolves before the spell with cascade). During cascade's resolution, you exile cards and may cast a noncreature spell without paying its mana cost. That spell is cast during the resolution of cascade (rule 608.2g: casting during resolution follows steps 601.2a–i, and no player gets priority after it's cast).
3. The cascaded noncreature spell becomes the topmost object on the stack (rule 608.2g).
4. **At this point, the cascaded spell has been cast**, so Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers (rule 702.108a: "Whenever you cast a noncreature spell..."). However, because we are still in the middle of resolving the cascade ability, triggered abilities are not put onto the stack yet (rule 608.2g: no player gets priority during resolution).
5. After cascade finishes resolving, all triggered abilities that triggered during its resolution (including prowess) are put onto the stack (rule 608.2p: abilities that trigger when a spell or ability resolves trigger after all steps are completed).
6. Prowess goes on the stack **on top of** the cascaded spell (Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2: prowess goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger).
7. Prowess resolves first, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 until end of turn, **before** the cascaded noncreature spell resolves.

Key definitions:
- **Prowess**: A triggered ability that gives +1/+1 until end of turn whenever you cast a noncreature spell (rule 702.108a).
- **Cascade**: A triggered ability that exiles cards until you exile a nonland card with lesser mana value, which you may cast without paying its mana cost (rule 702.85a).
- **Casting during resolution**: The spell is cast following normal rules, but no player gets priority after it's cast (rule 608.2g).

Thus, the prowess trigger will resolve before the cascaded noncreature spell resolves, even though the cascaded spell was cast first chronologically.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text: No, state-based actions do not make the Grizzly Bears die before Lightning Bolt resolves. State-based actions are only checked before a player would receive priority [704.3], not during the resolution of a spell or ability [704.4]. Lightning Bolt is a spell that uses the stack [117.2d]; once it begins resolving, the game does not check state-based actions until after the spell finishes resolving and a player would next receive priority [510.3a]. The Grizzly Bears has 2 damage marked on it, which is not lethal (its toughness is 2, so damage is not greater than or equal to toughness) [704.5g]. Even if the damage were lethal, the destruction would happen as a state-based action after Lightning Bolt resolves, not before. The key point is that state-based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell [704.4].

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text: Both triggers happen at the same time—at the beginning of the upkeep step. According to rule [603.2b], when a phase or step begins, all abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” that phase or step trigger simultaneously. Then, per [603.3b], the next time a player would receive priority (which is the active player getting priority at the start of the upkeep step, per [503.1a]), the triggered abilities are put onto the stack in a two-part process: first, each player in APNAP order puts their own triggered abilities on the stack in any order they choose. Since you are the active player, you put your Phyrexian Arena trigger on the stack first, choosing its order among any other triggers you control. Then your opponent, as the nonactive player, puts their trigger on the stack in any order they choose. The result is that your opponent’s trigger will be on top of the stack (resolving first) if you put your trigger on the stack first, or vice versa. The exact timing is that they trigger at the beginning of the upkeep step, and they are put on the stack just before the active player gets priority during that step.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text: Only the original sorcery card returns to your hand. The copy created by Fork is not a card and will cease to exist after it resolves, so it cannot go to your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text: No, you do not get a token. The face-down manifested Lightning Bolt is an instant card, not a creature card. When it dies and is exiled with Mimic Vat's imprint ability, it becomes a face-down exiled card. However, Mimic Vat's activated ability creates a token that is a copy of a card exiled with it. Since Lightning Bolt is an instant (a nonpermanent card), the token would be a copy of a nonpermanent card, and no token is created. This is explicitly stated in [Mimic Vat ruling #0]: "If the creature that dies is an instant or sorcery card that's been manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled. You can't create a token that's a copy of a nonpermanent card. No token is created in this case." Additionally, [111.12] confirms that if an effect instructs a player to create a token that is a copy of a nonexistent object (here, a nonpermanent card cannot be a token), no token is created. The face-down status of the exiled card does not change its underlying card type (instant), as per [406.3a] and [406.3b] which note that face-down exiled cards have no characteristics but the spell or ability that exiled them may allow them to be played; however, Mimic Vat's ability does not allow casting, only copying, and the copy fails because the card is nonpermanent.

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes, both exiled creatures return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. The two abilities are linked: Fiend Hunter's first ability (which exiles a creature) and its second ability (which returns "the exiled card") are linked abilities. When you copy the first ability with Lithoform Engine, the copy is also linked to the second ability. The second ability refers to all cards exiled by both the original and the copy. Therefore, when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its second ability returns both exiled creatures. This is confirmed by the Lithoform Engine ruling that explicitly states: if Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability is copied and two creatures are exiled, they both return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield. Banishing Light's one-shot effect that exiles the creature "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield" is waiting for Banishing Light to leave the battlefield. When Banishing Light phases out due to Teferi's Protection, it does not leave the battlefield—it remains on the battlefield but is treated as though it doesn't exist. Rule [702.26d] states that phasing does not cause a permanent to change zones, and zone-change triggers (like leaves-the-battlefield) do not trigger. Additionally, [Teferi's Protection ruling #21] explicitly says that one-shot effects waiting "until [this] leaves the battlefield" (such as Banishing Light's) won't happen when a permanent phases out. Therefore, the exiled creature stays exiled until Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield (e.g., by being destroyed, exiled, or returned to hand).

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text: No, your opponent cannot target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell while it is on the stack, because Emrakul has protection from instants. Protection from instants means Emrakul cannot be the target of instant spells (like Counterspell) while it is on the battlefield, but according to [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2], protection abilities only apply while the object with the ability is on the battlefield. However, that ruling specifically states that Emrakul *may* be the target of a spell that targets it while on the stack, such as Syncopate. This is because protection from instants is a static ability that functions only on the battlefield (see rule [610.5] for how static abilities apply to spells as they are cast, but protection is not a one-shot effect that applies during casting—it is a characteristic of the permanent). Since Emrakul is a spell on the stack, not a permanent, its protection ability does not apply, so Counterspell can legally target it. If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the spell is removed from the stack and does not resolve. The cast trigger from Emrakul ("When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn...") has already triggered and is on the stack separately. That trigger will still resolve even if Emrakul is countered, because the trigger is independent of the spell's resolution (see rule [603.1a] and [608.2m]). So yes, you will still control that opponent's next turn, and after that turn, that opponent takes an extra turn as specified. The answer to the question is: Yes, Counterspell can target Emrakul on the stack (protection does not apply there), and if countered, the cast trigger still resolves, giving you control of the opponent's next turn and them an extra turn after.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text: No, you cannot cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor via cascade from exiling Valki, God of Lies. Cascade checks the mana value of the card you exile, and for a double-faced card, the mana value is always calculated from the front face’s mana cost ([712.8c]). Valki’s front face has mana value 2, which is not less than your cascade spell’s mana value (since cascade requires the exiled nonland card’s mana value to be *less than* the cascade spell’s mana value, per [702.85a]). Additionally, cascade only allows you to cast the card itself, not a specific face; you could cast Valki (the front face) if its mana value were less than the cascade spell’s, but you cannot choose to cast the back face Tibalt instead ([712.11c], [712.11d]). The card’s ruling that you may cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits the criteria ([Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]) applies only when an effect allows casting from a group of cards, but cascade’s own restriction (mana value comparison) is not satisfied here because the card’s mana value is 2, not 7.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control one of your opponent's turns (from the original Emrakul cast trigger), and you will get a second Emrakul token from copying the permanent spell. Copying the Emrakul spell with Lithoform Engine does **not** give you another control-a-turn trigger, because the copy is not cast—it is put directly onto the stack as a copy, and the cast trigger only happens when you *cast* Emrakul.

Here is the step-by-step breakdown:

1. **Original Emrakul cast trigger**: When you cast Emrakul, its triggered ability goes on the stack: “When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.” This is a cast trigger ([Emrakul, the Promised End]'s oracle text).

2. **Copy the cast trigger with Lithoform Engine**: You activate Lithoform Engine's first ability ({2}, {T}) targeting the Emrakul cast trigger on the stack. Per [Lithoform Engine ruling #3], this creates another instance of that triggered ability on the stack. That copy resolves and gives you control of the same opponent's next turn and an extra turn for that opponent after that turn. However, [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14] says multiple player-controlling effects overwrite each other—the last one created works. Since both the original and the copy target the same opponent, the copy (being the last to resolve) will be the one that controls that opponent's next turn, and the original's effect is overwritten. The extra turn from the copy still happens after that controlled turn. So you end up controlling **one** of that opponent's turns (the next one they actually take), and they get one extra turn after that.

3. **Untap Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key**: You activate Voltaic Key ({1}, {T}) to untap Lithoform Engine. This is straightforward.

4. **Copy the Emrakul permanent spell with Lithoform Engine**: You activate Lithoform Engine's third ability ({4}, {T}) targeting the Emrakul spell on the stack. Per [Lithoform Engine ruling #5] and [Lithoform Engine ruling #6], this creates a copy of the permanent spell on the stack. The copy is not cast—it is put directly onto the stack. Per [111.13], when that copy resolves, it becomes a token that is a copy of Emrakul (a 13/13 Eldrazi with flying, trample, protection from instants). So you **do** get a second Emrakul token.

5. **Does copying the Emrakul spell give another control-a-turn trigger?** No. The control-a-turn ability is a triggered ability that triggers “When you cast this spell” ([Emrakul, the Promised End]'s oracle text). Since the copy of Emrakul is not cast ([707.10] and [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]), that trigger condition is not met. The copy simply enters the battlefield as a token with no cast trigger.

**Summary**: You control one of your opponent's turns (from the copied trigger), you get a second Emrakul token, and you do not get an additional control-a-turn trigger from copying the spell.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
No, you do not get two tokens. Here is the step-by-step reasoning:

1. **Mimic Vat’s activated ability** is put on the stack. It says: “Create a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with this artifact. It gains haste. Exile it at the beginning of the next end step.”

2. **Lithoform Engine’s first ability** targets that activated ability on the stack and creates a copy of it. Per [707.10b], the copy is put onto the stack, is controlled by you, and copies all decisions made for the original (including the fact that it refers to “a card exiled with this artifact”).

3. **Both the original ability and the copy resolve.** Each one tries to create a token that is a copy of a card exiled with Mimic Vat. However, the copy of the ability refers to the same Mimic Vat object as the original ability (see [707.10b]: “A copy of an ability has the same source as the original ability”). The source of the copy is the same Mimic Vat, not a different object. This is confirmed by [Lithoform Engine ruling #0]: “The source of the copy from Lithoform Engine’s first ability is the same as the source of the original ability.”

4. **When the first ability resolves**, it creates a token that is a copy of the exiled card. That token is a permanent on the battlefield. The token is not “a card exiled with this artifact” – it is a token, not a card, and it is not exiled with Mimic Vat.

5. **When the copy of the ability resolves**, it also looks for “a card exiled with this artifact.” The only card exiled with Mimic Vat is the original imprinted creature card. That card is still exiled. The copy of the ability does not see the token created by the first ability, because that token is not a card and is not exiled with Mimic Vat. Therefore, the copy of the ability creates a second token that is a copy of the same exiled card.

6. **Result**: You get two tokens, each a copy of the same exiled creature card. The key point is that the copy of the ability does not fail – it successfully creates a token because the exiled card still exists. The copy does not try to copy the token; it copies the exiled card.

**Important nuance**: If the first ability’s resolution had somehow removed the exiled card (e.g., if the token creation caused the exiled card to leave exile), then the copy of the ability would fail because there would be no card to copy. But Mimic Vat’s ability does not remove the exiled card; it only creates a token. So the exiled card remains, and the copy of the ability can use it.

Thus, you end up with two tokens, each a copy of the same imprinted creature card.

**Citations**: [707.10b], [707.10e], [Lithoform Engine ruling #0], [Mimic Vat ruling #4], [Mimic Vat ruling #6], [111.12]

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text: If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0, its mana cost is {0}{G}{G}. The cost reduction of {1} applies first, reducing the total cost to {G}{G}. Then Trinisphere's effect checks: the mana component of the cost is {G}{G} (2 mana), which is less than 3, so it becomes {3} (any three mana). You get zero tokens because X=0. To get any tokens, you must choose X such that after the {1} reduction and Trinisphere's minimum, the total cost is at least 3 mana. For example, with X=1, the mana cost is {1}{G}{G} (3 mana), reduced to {2}{G} (3 mana), which already meets 3, so Trinisphere does nothing and you get one token. With X=2, cost is {2}{G}{G} (4 mana), reduced to {1}{G}{G} (3 mana), still meets 3, you get two tokens. In short, X=0 costs {3} and yields 0 tokens; X=1 costs {2}{G} and yields 1 token; X=2 costs {1}{G}{G} and yields 2 tokens; X=3 costs {2}{G}{G} and yields 3 tokens, etc.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard with Animate Dead. Here is the step-by-step process and outcome:

1. **Targeting**: When you cast Animate Dead, you target Grist, the Hunger Tide card in your graveyard. This is legal because Grist is a creature card in the graveyard (per [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], anywhere but the battlefield it is a creature in addition to its other types).

2. **Animate Dead enters the battlefield**: Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to the targeted Grist card in the graveyard. Its triggered ability triggers: "When this Aura enters, if it's on the battlefield, it loses 'enchant creature card in a graveyard' and gains 'enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura.' Return enchanted creature card to the battlefield under your control and attach this Aura to it." (from Animate Dead's oracle text).

3. **Resolution of the triggered ability**: The ability resolves. It returns Grist from the graveyard to the battlefield under your control. At this point, Grist is a planeswalker on the battlefield (per [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1], once on the battlefield it is no longer a creature). Animate Dead then attaches to Grist (now a planeswalker on the battlefield) because its enchant ability has changed to "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura." However, Grist is no longer a creature, so Animate Dead cannot legally enchant it. According to [Animate Dead ruling #4], if the creature put onto the battlefield has protection from black—or if the creature can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead for another reason—Animate Dead won't be able to attach to it. It will be put into the graveyard as a state-based action, causing its delayed triggered ability to trigger. When the trigger resolves, if the creature's still on the battlefield, its controller will sacrifice it.

4. **State-based action**: Because Grist is not a creature on the battlefield, Animate Dead cannot be attached to it. State-based actions are checked (per [704.4] and [704.8]), and Animate Dead is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action (since an Aura attached to an illegal object or not attached to anything is put into its owner's graveyard).

5. **Delayed triggered ability**: Animate Dead's delayed triggered ability ("When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it") triggers and goes on the stack. When it resolves, you must sacrifice Grist (the "creature" referred to is the creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead, which is Grist). Grist is put into the graveyard.

**Final result**: Grist enters the battlefield briefly, then is sacrificed and returns to the graveyard. Animate Dead is also in the graveyard. Grist never becomes a creature on the battlefield; it remains a planeswalker while on the battlefield.

Key rules relied upon: [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1] (Grist is a creature card in graveyard), [Animate Dead ruling #4] (creature can't be enchanted leads to sacrifice), [Animate Dead ruling #0] (Animate Dead must be on battlefield for its ability to resolve), [Animate Dead ruling #1] (targeting creature card in graveyard), and the general rules for state-based actions and Aura attachment (implied by [704.4] and [704.8]).

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text: Skullbriar retains its four +1/+1 counters when it moves from the battlefield to the command zone (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3). When you recast it, it enters the battlefield as a new object with those counters still on it (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2). Doubling Season’s replacement effect applies to permanents entering with counters (Doubling Season ruling #2), so the four +1/+1 counters are doubled to eight as Skullbriar enters the battlefield (rule 614.16, rule 701.10e).

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. Final Fortune creates a delayed triggered ability that triggers 'at the beginning of that turn's end step.' When you activate Sundial of the Infinite to end the turn before the end step, the end step is skipped entirely. Because the end step never occurs, the delayed triggered ability never triggers, so you never lose the game. This is confirmed by the Final Fortune ruling: 'If you end up skipping the extra turn that is gained, you do not lose the game.' Although that ruling specifically mentions skipping the extra turn, the same principle applies when the end step of that turn is skipped — the trigger condition (beginning of the end step) never happens, so the ability never triggers. Additionally, rule [724.1e] states that when an effect ends the turn, 'at the beginning of the end step' triggered abilities don't trigger because the end step is skipped. Rule [724.1d] confirms that the game skips straight to the cleanup step, bypassing the end step. Therefore, the loss condition from Final Fortune does not occur.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text: You choose what Clone copies as it enters the battlefield, not as it is cast. The choice is made when the replacement effect from Clone's ability applies to the event of it entering the battlefield. This choice does not use the stack and cannot be responded to by your opponent. Specifically, Clone's ability is a static ability that creates a replacement effect (see [707.2] and [Clone ruling #0]). The choice of which creature to copy is made at the moment Clone would enter, as part of applying that replacement effect. Since it is not a spell or ability being cast or activated, there is no opportunity for players to respond with instants or abilities after the choice is made. The opponent cannot respond to the choice itself, though they may respond to the spell Clone before it resolves and enters the battlefield.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands total from that one Flooded Strand activation. Here's the breakdown:

- Flooded Strand's activated ability is put on the stack. When it resolves, you search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, and shuffle. That's one land.
- Gogo's ability targets that Flooded Strand ability on the stack and creates two copies of it (since X=2). Each copy is a separate instance of the ability on the stack. When each copy resolves, you search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, and shuffle. That's two more lands.
- The copies are not cast or activated; they are put directly onto the stack by Gogo's ability ([707.10b]). Each copy has the same characteristics and decisions as the original, including the search instruction ([707.10b]).
- The search instruction in each copy is a separate search event. Rule [701.23h] says that if an effect instructs a player to search a library more than once before shuffling, that's treated as a single search. However, here each copy is a separate ability on the stack, and each resolves independently. The original ability's search and shuffle happen during its resolution, and each copy's search and shuffle happen during its own resolution. They are not combined into one search.
- Therefore, you perform three separate searches (one from the original, two from the copies), each finding a land, and each followed by a shuffle of your library.

Key rules relied on: [707.10b] (copying an ability puts a copy on the stack, copies all decisions including targets and costs), [701.23h] (multiple searches before a single shuffle are combined, but here each ability is a separate event), and [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6] (Gogo creates additional instances of the ability on the stack).
